title: Linear and binary search: preconditions and boundaries
lead: Find a first match and a duplicate interval while proving the required ordering is available.
why: A fast search under the wrong order can return a convincing but incorrect answer. An index needs a key, duplicate policy, preparation cost and a clear meaning for returned positions.
objectives: Implement lower_bound with a half-open interval.
prerequisites: Modules 1–3: validated input, functions, vector, records, references and lifetimes.
Direct learning dependencies: cpp.iterators-algorithms-lambdas. New constructs are explained before the task.

sections.title: What does “find” mean?
paragraphs: Search can ask whether a key exists, where its first match is, how many matches exist, or which records satisfy a range. These answers are not interchangeable. For each target, the lab returns the target, its first matching index and its count; absence uses index −1 and count zero.

An index is a position in the current ordered collection, not a permanent record ID. Rearrangement can make an old position identify something else. Store a domain ID in the record and search for it again. Duplicate values may be allowed while duplicate IDs are rejected by a separate project contract.

sections.title: Linear search as a baseline oracle
paragraphs: A linear scan checks items in sequence and needs no sorting. Stop at the first equality for a first match, or continue to count all matches. This is easy to inspect on small data and makes a useful independent oracle for a more complex search. Do not reuse the very boundary defect you intend to check inside the oracle.

Absence requires inspecting all n items; a first-position match needs one equality check. For one query on a small collection, sorting a copy may cost more than scanning. Start with a correct simple solution and estimate how many queries could repay an index before calling binary search unconditionally better.

sections.title: Sorting is sufficient, but understand partitioning
paragraphs: For ascending lower_bound, element<target must hold on an initial segment and fail afterward. That is partitioning for the particular target. A fully sorted range supplies it for every target, so the lab requires sorting and checks is_sorted first. Arbitrary unsorted input does not give the algorithm a meaningful-result obligation.

Index construction and queries must use compatible ordering. Sorting records by name does not prepare an ID search. Silently sorting inside every query changes both cost and position meaning. Design the required index and specify when mutations require rebuilding it.

sections.title: A half-open lower-bound invariant
paragraphs: Maintain first=0 and last=n. Elements before first are known to be smaller than target; elements from last through n−1 are known not to be smaller. The insertion position lies between first and last, including both boundary positions. While first<last, mid=first+(last−first)/2 identifies a valid element to compare.

If a[mid]<target, the boundary is to its right, so set first=mid+1. Otherwise set last=mid because mid may itself be the first suitable position. Both branches strictly decrease last−first, proving termination. At first==last the boundary is found, but it can be n; reading a[n] remains invalid.

sections.title: Duplicates, upper bound and safe absence
paragraphs: lower_bound returns the first element not less than target; upper_bound returns the first strictly greater element. Their half-open interval contains all ties, and vector-iterator subtraction gives the count. On [1,2,2,2,9] for target 2 the positions are 1 and 4, giving three matches. For absent target 3 both boundaries equal 4.

Check whether the matching interval is empty before reading a record. With custom comparators, lower_bound calls comp(element,target), while upper_bound calls comp(target,element); this matters when searching structures with a numeric key. Successful compilation does not prove the two predicates describe the same order.

sections.title: Comparisons, advances and total cost
paragraphs: Each comparison roughly halves the candidates, giving logarithmic comparison growth. A vector supports constant-time midpoint access, allowing logarithmic search on a prepared range. A standard boundary search on a forward range can have logarithmic comparisons yet linear iterator advances. Do not call their total time identical from comparison counts alone.

The lab reads n values and q queries, validates input and ordering, then searches. Total processing includes O(n+q) reading and O(n) validation, not just O(q log n). A service reusing an index can account for preparation separately, but that must match the actual data lifecycle.

sections.title: How boundary logic fails
paragraphs: Using first=mid instead of mid+1 can leave a one-candidate interval unchanged. On paper, first=3,last=4 gives mid=3, so length does not decrease. There is no need to run an infinite loop in the working runtime: demonstrate the broken variant or simulate a bounded number of steps separately.

(first+last)/2 can overflow for large boundaries; first+(last−first)/2 avoids that problem under valid bounds. Do not mix half-open update rules with a closed interval or use size−1 on an empty array. Choose one convention and align every update, condition and final check with it.

sections.title: Tests and the transition to recursion
paragraphs: Compare the library interval with an independent linear count on empty, singleton, all-equal and mixed collections. Query before the minimum, the minimum, a duplicate, a gap, the maximum and after it. Unsorted input should be explicitly rejected, not yield an arbitrary position. Missing queries and extra tokens test the application contract too.

The cumulative practicum connects stable record sorting with boundary search under the same key. Keep original labels and explain preparation separately from querying. Recursion comes next: shrinking a subproblem remains central, but function calls store continuation state instead of only two loop variables.

workedExamples.title: Shrinking a half-open interval
workedExamples.purpose: Compare a manual lower bound with the library boundary on sorted input.
steps: first=0 and last=5; the boundary is one of the positions from 0 through 5.
At mid=2 the value equals 2, so the boundary is not to the right: last=2.
Equality at mid=1 gives last=1; value 1 at mid=0 is smaller, so first=1.
Now first==last==1. The boundary is found; i<size protects the later read when no match exists.
Try empty, singleton and unsorted input; the last is rejected before binary search.

workedExamples.title: Comparisons and advances are different counts
workedExamples.purpose: Count comparisons on a vector without transferring its access cost to a list.
steps: The vector contains 128 even values 0…254; the boundary for 127 is 64.
Each step counts one comparison a[mid]<127, not every instruction.
The first step chooses index 64; later comparisons exclude the remaining candidates.
Seven comparisons confirm this trace; another target can require eight.
Advancing a forward iterator to a midpoint is not constant time, so equal comparison counts do not imply equal advancement counts.

blockPracticum.title: Practicum: a ranking and a tied-key interval
blockPracticum.challenge: Read n and target followed by n integer keys. Require 0≤n≤32 and every value in −10000…10000. Print a stable sort as key:original-index, then first count for target, with first=−1 when absent. Reject incomplete or extra input as invalid.
walkthrough: Capture the original position before sorting; otherwise stability has no observable evidence. Binary search uses exactly the key that defines the sorted order.
Write the comparator signatures for lower_bound and upper_bound: argument order differs. Explain why first==last denotes an empty group, not permission to dereference end.
